headline: Rough Riders roll toward Tampa
summary: On a long, sweltering, crowded train ride to Florida, Roosevelt lets his troopers drink but comes down hard on anyone who gets drunk. In spare moments he reads a French book on Anglo-Saxon superiority.

events.detail: Regiment travels by rail toward Tampa
Allows drinking among the men but disciplines drunkenness at once
Reads a French-language book on the supposed superiority of the Anglo-Saxons

uncertain: The book title is hard to read in the record; it is likely Edmond Demolins's A quoi tient la superiorite des Anglo-Saxons.

headline: Hot coffee on a hungry train
summary: With no hot meals aboard, Roosevelt arranges hot coffee for his troopers. At station stops along the way, townspeople hand the soldiers watermelons and beer.

events.detail: Train continues toward Tampa
Has hot coffee brought to the troopers, who get no hot meals
Locals at station stops give the troops watermelons and beer

headline: Into the chaos at Tampa
summary: The regiment arrives at Tampa to find the railroads in a snarl; the troopers ride the last six miles and Roosevelt and Wood hunt for their campsite after dark in 90-degree heat. Edith has come down to the Tampa Bay Hotel, and he spends the night there with her.

events.detail: Reaches Tampa, where 25,000 troops are gathering
Takes twelve hours to get the regiment and baggage into camp; Roosevelt and Wood locate the campground in darkness
Stays the night with Edith at the Tampa Bay Hotel during her four-day visit

tr_quotes.text: Reached Tampa in morning. Railway system in wildest confusion; it took us twelve hours to get into camp with our baggage.
(E. [Edith] came down for 4 lovely days.)

uncertain: The note about Edith's four-day visit is an undated diary entry.

headline: Weary horses, drill on foot
summary: The horses are worn out from the trip, so the regiment drills on foot. Roosevelt rides into Tampa, and Edith writes home to the children.

events.detail: Regiment drills on foot because the horses are exhausted
Rides into town
Edith writes to the children

tr_quotes.text: Horses very tired. Drilled on foot.

headline: A diary cry over Tampa's disorder
summary: Roosevelt pours his frustration into his diary, blaming the mess at Tampa on a collapse of both the rail and military systems. Edith writes her sister Emily about her journey to Florida.

events.detail: Diary entry condemns the disorder at Tampa
Edith writes to Emily Carow about traveling to Florida

tr_quotes.text: No word can paint the confusion. No head; a breakdown of both the railroad & military system of the country.

headline: Mounted drill and hard news
summary: The Rough Riders show off a sharp mounted drill on the flats, watched by foreign military observers, Richard Harding Davis and Edith. Then word comes that only officers' horses will ship to Cuba, and just eight of the regiment's twelve troops will go.

events.detail: Mounted drill on the flats impresses foreign attachés
Learns that troopers' horses stay behind and troops C, H, I and M will not sail
Writes Lodge, the correspondent John W. Fox and his children

letters.topic: Edith's visit to camp and getting ready to leave for Cuba
Welcomes Fox to join as a correspondent any time
Their mother at camp; the journey from San Antonio

tr_quotes.text: Mounted drill, very good, much admired by foreign attaches.
No plans; no staff officers; no instructions to us. Each officer finds out for himself & takes his chances. We are doing as well as the regular regiments. Have very light baggage.
whenever you wish.

headline: Edith heads home; orders to embark
summary: Edith starts back to New York. Drinking coffee in the hotel, Roosevelt hears the troops will ship out right away, and he dashes off notes to his sisters brimming with eagerness to go.

events.detail: Edith returns to New York
Stops at the Tampa Bay Hotel for coffee
Learns the expedition is to embark at once
Writes to Corinne and Bamie

letters.topic: The regiment is about to board ship for Cuba
Determination not to be left behind

tr_quotes.text: We are at the point of embarking for Cuba.
We would rather crawl on all fours than not go.

headline: Seizing a coal train and a ship
summary: When no train shows up, Roosevelt commandeers a coal train going the wrong way and has it backed down to the docks with his men aboard. Wood grabs the transport Yucatan, meant for two other regiments, and the Rough Riders hold it. Two Vitagraph cameramen come along; the fleet sails but halts on reports of ships in the Gulf.

events.detail: Commandeers a coal train and runs it in reverse to the landing
Wood takes over the transport Yucatan; the regiment keeps other units off
Two Vitagraph motion-picture cameramen board the ship
Transports set out but stop after possibly Spanish vessels are reported

tr_quotes.text: Told to go aboard transport. Worst confusion yet. R.R. system utterly mismanaged. No allotment of transports. Utter confusion.

uncertain: The record marks it as uncertain whether the ships sighted were Spanish.

headline: Packed aboard and going nowhere
summary: The troopers sit crammed aboard the Yucatan in the heat, waiting without complaint while the food goes bad. Roosevelt fumes in his diary about the bungling.

events.detail: Men wait in cramped, hot quarters as rations spoil
Diary entry on the delay and mismanagement

tr_quotes.text: After we were embarked had us stay still! and the maladministration here beats everything.

headline: Sharks and swimmers in midstream
summary: The transports move out into the channel. Sharks prowl the water, but some overheated men go swimming anyway. Roosevelt tells Lodge the disorder is beyond words.

events.detail: Transports shift into midstream
Some troopers swim despite sharks
Writes Lodge about the mismanagement

letters.topic: The disorder and mismanagement at Tampa

tr_quotes.text: No words could describe to you the confusion and lack of system and the general mismanagement of affairs here.

headline: Baking in the harbor
summary: Another day stalled in Tampa harbor. Roosevelt notes in his diary that the tropical sun is hard on his men.

events.detail: Transports remain idle in the harbor

tr_quotes.text: Delay in harbor under the tropical sun very bad for men.

headline: Sixth day aboard the sweltering ship
summary: Still stuck in the bay, Roosevelt writes Bamie about a small ship carrying a thousand men, warns Edith the wait is hurting morale, and asks Lodge to carry word of the Tampa mismanagement to the President.

events.detail: Ship remains anchored in the bay
Letters to Bamie, Edith and Lodge

letters.topic: Six days cramped aboard a small, overcrowded transport
Fears the long delay will hurt the men
Asks Lodge to tell the President about mismanagement at Tampa

tr_quotes.text: Still in bay.
This is our sixth day sweltering on this troop ship under the semitropical sun in Tampa harbor. It is not a large ship and has a thousand men aboard.
If we are kept here much longer it cannot fail to have a bad effect on the men.

uncertain: The record notes that this letter, addressed to Corinne, was really written to Edith.

headline: Anchors up, then down again
summary: In the afternoon the transports finally raise anchor, move down the bay and drop anchor once more.

events.detail: Transports shift down the bay and anchor

tr_quotes.text: Transports weighed anchor in afternoon; went down bay & anchored.

headline: At last, the fleet sails for Cuba
summary: The transports clear the Tampa Bay lighthouse and steam for Cuba that evening, every ship lit up while the bands play the national anthem together. Roosevelt sends Douglas Robinson a quick note.

events.detail: Fleet passes the Tampa Bay lighthouse and sails for Cuba
Bands on the lighted ships all strike up the national anthem together
Note to Douglas Robinson

letters.topic: They are on the point of sailing

tr_quotes.text: Left Tampa Bay lighthouse in afternoon.
We are about to sail.

uncertain: Guest-book entry (James K. Gracie) is at Sagamore Hill, not with TR.

headline: Lights off Key West
summary: Late in the evening Roosevelt spots the lights of the Tortugas and Key West. The 31-ship convoy stretches 25 miles and straggles, and General Shafter brushes off the Navy's plea to darken the ships at night.

events.detail: Convoy passes the Dry Tortugas and Key West
Shafter refuses the Navy's request to keep the ships dark
Note to Edith

letters.topic: The convoy is steaming south

tr_quotes.text: Late in Evening saw Tortuga lights & those on Key West
Steaming southward

uncertain: The record notes that this letter, addressed to Corinne, was really written to Edith.

headline: Slow going, school at sea
summary: The convoy crawls along, slowed by a schooner and a scow under tow. By day the officers hold classes and the men drill on deck.

events.detail: Fleet makes slow progress because of vessels in tow
Drill and an officers' school held on board

tr_quotes.text: Progress very slow, chiefly because of the follow which has caused schooner and a scow to be towed.

headline: At sea
summary: Another day aboard ship on the way to Cuba; the record notes nothing more.

events.detail: Continues at sea toward Cuba

headline: Sent back to guard a straggler
summary: Shafter orders the Yucatan back to escort a transport towing a schooner. Roosevelt calls the order idiotic: his ship has no towline and only gives the rear gunboat Bancroft one more vessel to watch.

events.detail: Ordered back to convoy a transport towing a schooner

tr_quotes.text: Sent back by Shafter to convoy another transport which is towing a schooner. This is simply idiotic. We cannot help the other transport in any way, as we have no tow rope, and the schooner would be towed under if she went any faster. We merely add another ship for the Bancroft, the rear gunboat, to protect.

headline: Left behind with the schooner
summary: The Yucatan plods along beside the towed schooner while the rest of the fleet disappears over the horizon.

events.detail: Keeps company with the schooner; main fleet out of sight

tr_quotes.text: In company with towed schooner; fleet out of sight ahead.

headline: Santiago is the target
summary: The fleet turns southwest and the destination becomes clear: Santiago. The ships stop some 20 miles to the east of Morro Castle after a day hugging the Cuban shore.

events.detail: Fleet stops off Santiago, some 20 miles to the east of Morro Castle
Writes Edith about the coast

letters.topic: A day steaming close along the Cuban coast

tr_quotes.text: Reach Santiago.
All day we have steamed close to the Cuban coast.

uncertain: The record notes that this letter, addressed to Corinne, was really written to Edith.

headline: Battle orders and a war dance
summary: Orders for the landing are read out to the troops, and Roosevelt celebrates with a war dance and a rousing Irish-American song.

events.detail: Battle orders announced aboard ship
Roosevelt dances and sings in celebration

headline: Ashore in Cuba with a toothbrush
summary: After a 3:30 a.m. reveille and a morning naval bombardment, the landing begins. Officers' horses are pushed overboard to swim; Roosevelt's Rain-in-the-Face drowns while Texas reaches shore. The Yucatan sails off with the baggage, leaving him only a toothbrush and a yellow mackinaw. By midnight 6,000 troops are on the beach.

events.detail: Ships shell the coast around Siboney while bands play

tr_quotes.text: Landed

uncertain: The record says the ships bombarded Siboney but does not name the landing beach, usually given as Daiquiri.

headline: Marching to Siboney
summary: After General Lawton seizes Siboney that morning, the regiment sets out at 3:45 p.m. under General Joseph Wheeler and cover seven steamy miles by sundown, Roosevelt on foot beside his men. Movie cameras catch pack mules on the trail toward Santiago.

events.detail: Lawton's troops capture Siboney

tr_quotes.text: Marched

headline: Under fire at Las Guasimas
summary: Before dawn the regiment pushes toward Las Guasimas, and Spanish snipers open up from cover, killing Sergeant Hamilton Fish and Captain Allyn Capron. Roosevelt, splinters in his eyes, leads three troops on a flanking fire that opens the way for the charge. In two hours the Spanish fall back, and he pockets three Mauser cartridges for his children.

events.detail: Battle of Las Guasimas begins with Spanish ambush
Leads three troops on the flank while Wood leads three; Davis points out enemy trenches
Bullets strike a tree and splinters fly into his eyes
Fish and Capron among those killed; correspondent Edward Marshall paralyzed by a wound
Collects three Spanish cartridges as souvenirs for his children
Fight ends about 9:20 a.m. with the Spanish in retreat

tr_quotes.text: Fight - Las Guasimas (7). We drove enemy in fine shape. Lost 60 men killed & wounded, 20 slight.

uncertain: Casualty figures differ within the record (TR's diary vs. the compiled totals). The record names only 'Young'; identifying him as Samuel B. M. Young comes from other sources.

headline: A day of rest after the fight
summary: The regiment rests. Roosevelt writes Edith an account of the Las Guasimas fight.

headline: Eleven hundred pounds of beans
summary: The regiment moves three miles. Told the commissary's beans are for officers only, Roosevelt orders 1,100 pounds of them as an officer, feeds his whole regiment, and hauls one sack himself over eight miles of jungle road.

headline: Scouting while the papers cheer
summary: The regiment stays put while Roosevelt goes out scouting. Back home the newspapers praise the Rough Riders and ignore the other units at Las Guasimas. Letters pass between him and Edith, and he writes Lodge about the battle.

letters.topic: News from camp

headline: Governor talk begins at home
summary: The Rough Riders remain on the Las Guasimas ridge. In New York, people are already talking about making Roosevelt the next governor.

headline: Back to the coast for supplies

headline: Night march toward San Juan
summary: Shafter surveys the heights of San Juan from El Pozo and holds a war council; the advance on Santiago begins as Wheeler falls ill with fever. The regiment marches late and camps at 9 p.m. At Sagamore Hill, Edith buys a horse she names Cuba and fills scrapbooks with clippings.

events.detail: Shafter surveys the heights of San Juan and holds a war council
Wheeler is struck by fever

tr_quotes.text: Marched late in afternoon. Camped at 9 p.m.

uncertain: The record's table of U.S. units in Cuba is hard to read and is left out.

headline: The charge up Kettle and San Juan hills
summary: Roosevelt's 'crowded hour.' With Wood moved up to brigade command, he leads the Rough Riders. After hours pinned down by fire at Bloody Ford, he rides Little Texas up Kettle Hill, takes a graze on the elbow, and finishes on foot. He then rallies the men across to San Juan Hill, where the flag is already up. The regiment suffers the heaviest losses of any unit there.

events.detail: Command reorganized: Sumner leads the cavalry division, Wood a brigade, Roosevelt the regiment
Spanish artillery answers the American guns; a shrapnel fragment strikes his wrist
Regiment waits under sniper fire at Bloody Ford; William O'Neill among the dead
Leads the charge up Kettle Hill on Little Texas, then on foot after a bullet grazes his elbow
Directs volley fire, then leads men, joined by troopers of the 1st and 10th regiments, to the top of San Juan Hill
The Rough Riders lose 89 men killed, 37 percent casualties

letters.topic: Urges him to come home safely

tr_quotes.text: The great day of my life.
Rose at 4. Big battle. Commanded regiment. Held extreme front of firing line.
All men who feel any power of joy in battle know what it is like when the wolf rises in the heart.
Are you afraid to stand up when I am on horseback?
Then let my men through, Sir!
Look at all these damned Spanish dead.

uncertain: The figure of 89 killed is as given in the record. The record's 'Bucky O'Neil' is rendered here as William O. O'Neill.

headline: Holding the ridge under shellfire
summary: Before dawn a shell lands near Roosevelt, who keeps striding the San Juan ridge under rifle and artillery fire. His diary lists officers of the regular cavalry. Bob Ferguson writes Edith that he now believes nothing can kill her husband.

events.detail: Under shell and rifle fire on the San Juan ridge
Records in his diary a list of regular cavalry officers

tr_quotes.text: Under shell & rifle fire.

uncertain: The diary's list of officers is hard to read in the record and is not quoted. The guest-book entries are at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Truce, and the Spanish fleet is gone
summary: A truce takes hold at noon. Off Santiago, the Navy under Sampson and Schley destroys the Spanish squadron as it runs for the open sea. Roosevelt's men dig in through daily rain, and he writes Edith and urges Lodge to get more troops and supplies sent.

events.detail: Truce declared at noon
U.S. fleet under Sampson and Schley destroys the Spanish squadron leaving Santiago harbor
Troops improve the trenches around Santiago
Writes Edith and Lodge

letters.topic: News from the front
Pleads for more men and supplies

tr_quotes.text: Truce at noon.
Spanish fleet destroyed.

headline: A grim Fourth in the trenches
summary: The truce holds, but men in the trenches suffer from wounds, dysentery, malaria and hunger. Army bands play for them, and the Rough Riders ask for 'Fair Harvard.' Across the Pacific, the U.S. takes Wake Island. Roosevelt sends Wood a report on what has happened since the July 1 battle.

letters.topic: What has happened since the July 1 battle

tr_quotes.text: Truce. Mismanagement horrible. No head to army.
